Myths that sound scientific

"Eat popcorn": the subliminal advertising that never happened

In 1957 an advertiser claimed he had boosted a cinema's sales with hidden messages. He had made it up.

In 1957, James Vicary announced that he had flashed the messages "Eat popcorn" and "Drink Coca-Cola" for a fraction of a second in a New Jersey cinema. According to him, popcorn sales rose 57% and soft drink sales 18%. The news caused alarm, and several countries banned subliminal advertising.

A confession

Nobody could reproduce the result and Vicary never published any data. In 1962 he admitted in an interview that the study had been invented to save his business.

Do subliminal effects exist? In the laboratory, very brief stimuli can have a small, short-lived influence, for example on choosing a drink when someone is already thirsty. But there is no evidence that they can make us buy something we do not want or change our beliefs.

References

  1. Pratkanis, A. R. (1992). The cargo-cult science of subliminal persuasion. Skeptical Inquirer, 16(3), 260–272.
  2. Karremans, J. C., Stroebe, W. y Claus, J. (2006). Beyond Vicary's fantasies. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 42(6), 792–798.
